Meanwhile, gravity would grow steadily weaker, decreasing in proportion to the square of the distance. My speed would therefore increase enormously until I reached the distant region where the moon’s pull would become stronger than the earth’s. With this reasoning in mind, I saw no reason to burden myself with more food than I would need for forty days.

“There was, however, one further difficulty that caused me some concern. People rising to great heights in balloons have reported more than painful breathing. They also suffer severe discomfort in the head and body, often with nosebleeds and other alarming symptoms. These troubles grow worse the higher they go. This was a rather frightening thought. Was it not likely that such symptoms would keep increasing, perhaps until death ended them? In the end, I decided they would not. Their cause, I reasoned, was the gradual loss of the normal air pressure against the body, which allowed the blood vessels near its surface to swell. They did not indicate an actual breakdown of the body’s workings. Difficulty in breathing was different: there, the air was chemically too thin to renew the blood properly in a chamber of the heart. Except for the failure of this renewal, I could see no reason why life should not continue even in a vacuum. The expansion and contraction of the chest, commonly called breathing, is simply a muscular movement. It causes the process of respiration rather than being caused by it. In short, I thought the pain would gradually fade as my body grew used to the lack of air pressure. While it lasted, I confidently trusted my exceptionally strong constitution to bear it.

“Thus, if it pleases your Excellencies, I have explained some, though by no means all, of the thoughts that led me to plan a journey to the moon. I shall now describe the outcome of an attempt that seemed so daring in its conception and was, in any case, entirely without precedent in human history.

“On reaching the height already mentioned—three and three-quarter miles—I tossed a quantity of feathers out of the balloon’s basket. From them I could tell that I was still rising quickly enough, so there was no need to throw out any ballast. This pleased me, because I wanted to keep as much weight with me as I could carry. My reasons for doing so will become clear later in this account.

And I summon you, spirits of the departed, and you, roaming agents of revenge, to assist and guide me in my labour. May the accursed, infernal monster drink his fill of anguish; may he know the despair that tortures me now.”

I had opened my invocation with solemnity and a reverence that almost convinced me the spirits of my murdered friends listened to and approved my dedication. But as I finished, the furies seized me, and wrath stifled my voice.

Out of the silence of the night came my answer: a loud, diabolical laugh. Long and ponderously it sounded in my ears; the mountains repeated it, and I seemed encircled by the derision and laughter of all hell. Surely at that instant madness would have mastered me and I would have ended my wretched life, had my oath not been heard and had I not been preserved for revenge. As the laughter faded, a familiar and detested voice, seemingly beside my ear, spoke in a whisper I could distinctly hear: “I am content, miserable creature! You have resolved to live, and I am content.”

I sprang towards the place whence the voice had come, but the demon escaped my hands. Suddenly the moon’s broad disk rose, lighting his hideous, misshapen figure fully as he fled at a speed beyond that of man.

I followed him, and this pursuit has occupied me for many months. Led by a slender clue, I traced the windings of the Rhone, yet without success. The blue Mediterranean came into view, and through a strange chance I saw the fiend steal aboard a vessel by night and conceal himself; the ship was bound for the Black Sea. I booked passage on that same vessel, but he slipped away, by what means I cannot tell.

Through the wildernesses of Tartary and Russia I have kept upon his trail, though he has continued to elude me. At times peasants, terrified by the dreadful apparition, told me which way he had gone. At others he himself left a sign to direct me, fearing that, should I lose every trace of him, I would despair and perish. Snow fell upon my head, and across the white plain I saw the imprint of his enormous foot. You, just beginning life, with care still new and agony unfamiliar, how can you comprehend what I have suffered and still suffer? Hunger, cold, and weariness were the smallest of my appointed torments. Some devil had cursed me, and I bore my everlasting hell wherever I went. Yet a benevolent spirit still attended and guided my steps, suddenly delivering me from difficulties that appeared unconquerable just when I complained most bitterly. Sometimes, when hunger overcame nature and I sank exhausted, a meal lay ready for me in the wilderness, renewing both my strength and my courage.

Soul and body, body and soul—what mysteries they were! The soul held animal instincts, and the body could experience moments of spiritual feeling. The senses could elevate a person, while the intellect could drag one down. Who could tell where a physical urge ended and a mental impulse began? The rigid definitions of ordinary psychologists seemed so shallow. Yet how hard it was to judge between their different schools of thought! Was the soul a shadow living in a sinful body? Or did the body actually exist inside the soul, as Giordano Bruno believed? Spirit’s separation from matter was a mystery, and so was their union.

He began to wonder whether psychology could ever become an exact enough science to reveal every small force that moves us through life. At present, we constantly misunderstood ourselves and seldom understood anyone else. Experience had no moral value. It was simply the name people gave their mistakes. Moral teachers generally treated it as a warning. They claimed it helped shape good character and praised it for teaching us what to pursue and what to avoid. But experience had no power to move us. It did no more to make us act than conscience did. All it truly showed was that our future would repeat our past, and that a sin we had committed once with disgust we would commit many times with pleasure.

To him, it was clear that only experiments could lead to a scientific understanding of the passions. Dorian Gray was certainly an ideal subject, one who seemed likely to yield rich and rewarding discoveries. His sudden, wild love for Sibyl Vane was a psychological event of considerable interest. Curiosity undoubtedly played a large part in it, along with a longing for new experiences. Yet the feeling was complex, far from simple. Whatever came from the purely physical instincts of youth had been altered by his imagination. It had become something that seemed to the boy himself to have little connection with the senses, making it all the more dangerous. The passions that ruled us most powerfully were those whose origins we hid from ourselves. The motives that had least power over us were those whose nature we understood. Often, when we believed we were experimenting on other people, we were actually experimenting on ourselves.

As Lord Henry sat lost in these thoughts, someone knocked at the door. His valet came in and reminded him that it was time to dress for dinner.
